---
<!-- mainthm-1: body_md -->
\label{main:thm}
  Let \( A \) be a finite-dimensional local algebra over a splitting field.
  If \( A \) admits two irreducible tensor factorizations
  \[
    A \cong P_1 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \cong Q_1 \otimes \dotsb \otimes Q_m,
  \]
  then \( n = m \) and, after reordering indices, \( P_i \cong Q_i \) for every \( i \).
<!-- end mainthm-1 -->
<!-- maincor-1: body_md -->
\label{main:cor}
  Let \( A, B, C \) be finite-dimensional local algebras over a splitting field.
  Then
  \[
    A \otimes C \cong B \otimes C \implies A \cong B.
  \]
<!-- end maincor-1 -->
<!-- dfn-1: body_md -->
Let \( Q \) be an algebra and let \( \beta \colon Q \to Q \) be an endomorphism.
  \index{\( \beta \) : Homomorphism} 
  By Fitting's lemma, there exists a least \( k \geq 1 \) such that \( Q = \operatorname{Im} \beta^k \oplus \operatorname{Ker} \beta^k \).
  \index{\( k \) : Integer} 
  We write
  \[
    X_\beta = \operatorname{Im} \beta^k
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    \varpi_{X_\beta} \colon Q \to X_\beta
  \]
  \index{\( X_\beta \) : Algebra} 
  \index{\( \varpi_{X_\beta} \) : Homomorphism} 
  for the projection along \( \operatorname{Ker} \beta^k \).
  Also we write
  \[
    Y_\beta = Q/Q \beta^k(J_Q) Q
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    \varpi_{Y_\beta} \colon Q \to Y_\beta
  \]
  for the canonical projection.
  \index{\( Y_\beta \) : Algebra} 
  \index{\( \varpi_{Y_\beta} \) : Homomorphism}
<!-- end dfn-1 -->
<!-- hyp-1: body_md -->
\label{hyp:common}
  Let \( B \), \( C \), \( Q \) be local algebras over a splitting field.
  Let \( \rho \colon B \otimes C \to Q \) be a retraction with a section \( \sigma \colon Q \to B \otimes C \).
  Define the homomorphisms \( \beta \colon Q \to Q \) and \( \gamma \colon Q \to Q \) by \( \beta = \rho\iota_B\pi_B\sigma \) and \( \gamma = \rho\iota_C\pi_C\sigma \).
  \index{\( \gamma \) : Homomorphism} 
  Set \( X = X_\beta \) and \( Y = Y_\beta \).
  \index{\( X \) : Algebra} 
  \index{\( Y \) : Algebra} 
  Define the homomorphism \( \alpha \colon Q \to X \otimes Y \) by \( \alpha = (\varpi_X\rho\iota_B \otimes \varpi_Y\rho\iota_C)\sigma \).
  \index{\( \alpha \) : Homomorphism}
<!-- end hyp-1 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:ImKer}
  Under \cref{hyp:common}, the following hold for some \( k \geq 1 \).
  \begin{itemize}
    \item[(a)] \( T_Q = \operatorname{Im} T_{\beta^k} + \operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k} \).
    \item[(b)] \( T_{\varpi_X\beta}(\operatorname{Im} T_{\beta^k}) = T_X \).
    \item[(c)] \( T_{\varpi_Y\gamma}(\operatorname{Im} T_{\beta^k}) = 0 \).
    \item[(d)] \( T_{\varpi_X\beta}(\operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k}) = 0 \).
    \item[(e)] \( T_{\varpi_Y\gamma}(\operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k}) = T_Y \).
  \end{itemize}
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By Fitting's lemma, there exists a least \( k \geq 1 \) such that \( Q = \operatorname{Im} \beta^k \oplus \operatorname{Ker} \beta^k \).
  Since \( T_{\iota_B\pi_B} + T_{\iota_C\pi_C} = \operatorname{id}_{T_{B \otimes C}} \) and \( T_{\rho\sigma} = \operatorname{id}_{T_Q} \), we have
  \[
    T_\beta + T_\gamma
    = T_\rho(T_{\iota_B\pi_B} + T_{\iota_C\pi_C})T_{\sigma}
    = \operatorname{id}_{T_Q}.
  \]

  (a)
  This follows from \( q = \varpi_X(q) + (q - \varpi_X(q)) \) for \( q \in J_Q \).
  \index{\( q \) : Element} 

  (b)
  This is clear from \( \varpi_X\beta^{k + 1}(J_Q) = J_X \).

  (c)
  Since \( \varpi_Y\beta^k(J_Q) = 0 \), this follows from \( T_{\varpi_Y\gamma\beta^k} = T_{\varpi_Y}(\operatorname{id}_{T_Q} - T_\beta)T_{\beta^k} = 0 \).

  (d)
  Since \( \beta \) is bijective on \( X \), this follows from \( \operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k} \subseteq \operatorname{Ker} T_{\varpi_X\beta^k} = \operatorname{Ker} T_{\varpi_X\beta} \).

  (e)
  Since \( T_\gamma = \operatorname{id}_{T_Q} - T_\beta \), we have \( T_\gamma(\operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k}) = \operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k} \).
  Then \( \varpi_Y\beta^k(J_Q) = 0 \) and (a) yield \( T_{\varpi_Y\gamma}(\operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k}) = T_{\varpi_Y}(\operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k}) = T_{\varpi_Y}(T_Q) = T_Y \).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:surj}
  Under \cref{hyp:common}, \( \alpha \colon Q \to X \otimes Y \) is surjective.
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
It suffices to prove that \( T_{X \otimes Y} = \operatorname{Im} T_\alpha \).
  Observe that
  \[
    T_\alpha = T_{\iota_X\varpi_X\beta} + T_{\iota_Y\varpi_Y\gamma}
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    T_{\iota_X\pi_X} + T_{\iota_Y\pi_Y} = \operatorname{id}_{T_{X \otimes Y}}.
  \]
  For some \( k \geq 1 \), by \cref{lem:ImKer}, we have
  \begin{align*}
    \operatorname{Im} T_\alpha
    &= T_\alpha(\operatorname{Im} T_{\beta^k}) + T_\alpha(\operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k}) \\
    &= T_{\iota_X\varpi_X\beta}(\operatorname{Im} T_{\beta^k}) + T_{\iota_Y\varpi_Y\gamma}(\operatorname{Ker} T_{\beta^k}) \\
    &= \operatorname{Im} T_{\iota_X} + \operatorname{Im} T_{\iota_Y} \\
    &= T_{X \otimes Y}.
    \qedhere
  \end{align*}
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:dim}
  Under \cref{hyp:common}, \( \dim Q \leq \dim X \dim Y \).
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
\cref{lem:ImKer}(e) implies \( \operatorname{Im} T_{\varpi_Y\gamma} = T_Y \) and hence \( \operatorname{Im} \varpi_Y\gamma = Y \).
  Set \( \ell = \dim Y \) and choose \( q_1, \dotsc, q_\ell \in \gamma(Q) \) such that \( \varpi_Y(q_1), \dotsc, \varpi_Y(q_\ell) \) form a basis of \( Y \).
  \index{\( l \) @ \( \ell \) : Integer} 
  \index{\( q_1, \dotsc, q_\ell \) : Elements} 
  By definition of \( X \) and \( Y \),
  \[
    Q = X q_1 + \dotsb + X q_\ell + Q J_X Q.
  \]
  Since every element of \( J_X \subseteq \rho\iota_B(B) \) commutes with \( q_1, \dotsc, q_\ell \in \rho\iota_C(C) \) and \( J_Q \) is nilpotent, iterating the above yields
  \begin{align*}
    Q
    &= X q_1 + \dotsb + X q_\ell + Q J_X Q \\
    &= X q_1 + \dotsb + X q_\ell + (Q J_X Q)^2 \\
    &\vdotswithin{=} \\
    &= X q_1 + \dotsb + X q_\ell.
  \end{align*}
  Hence \( \dim Q \leq \dim X \dim Y \).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:factor}
  Under \cref{hyp:common}, \( Q \cong X \otimes Y \).
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The homomorphism \( \alpha \colon Q \to X \otimes Y \) is an isomorphism by \cref{lem:surj,lem:dim}.
  Hence \( Q \cong X \otimes Y \).
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:avoid}
  Let \( B \), \( C \), \( Q \) be local algebras over a splitting field.
  Assume that \( Q \) is irreducible.
  If \( \rho \colon B \otimes C \to Q \) is a retraction, then \( \rho\iota_B \colon B \to Q \) or \( \rho\iota_C \colon C \to Q \) is a retraction.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let \( \sigma \colon Q \to B \otimes C \) be a section of \( \rho \).
  Define the homomorphisms \( \beta \colon Q \to Q \) and \( \gamma \colon Q \to Q \) by \( \beta = \rho\iota_B\pi_B\sigma \) and \( \gamma = \rho\iota_C\pi_C\sigma \).
  Note that \( T_Q \) is non-zero as \( Q \) is non-trivial.
  Since \( T_{\iota_B\pi_B} + T_{\iota_C\pi_C} = \operatorname{id}_{T_{B \otimes C}} \) and \( T_{\rho\sigma} = \operatorname{id}_{T_Q} \), we have
  \[
    T_\beta + T_\gamma
    = T_\rho(T_{\iota_B\pi_B} + T_{\iota_C\pi_C})T_{\sigma}
    = \operatorname{id}_{T_Q}.
  \]
  In particular, \( T_\beta \) and \( T_\gamma \) commute and at least one of them is not nilpotent.
  We may assume that it is \( T_\beta \).

  By \cref{prop:factor}, \( X_\beta \) is a tensor factor of \( Q \).
  Since \( T_\beta \) is not nilpotent and \( Q \) is irreducible, \( X_\beta \) is non-trivial and isomorphic to \( Q \).
  Then \( \beta \) is bijective and a section of \( \rho\iota_B \) is given by \( \pi_B\sigma\beta^{-1} \).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:first}
  Let \( P_1, \dotsc, P_n \), \( Q \), \( R \) be local algebras over a splitting field.
  \index{\( R \) : Algebra} 
  Assume that \( Q \) is irreducible and there exists an isomorphism
  \[
    \varphi \colon P_1 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \to Q \otimes R.
  \]
  Then \( \pi_Q\varphi\iota_B \colon B \to Q \) is surjective for some \( B \) among \( P_1, \dotsc, P_n \).
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Define the homomorphisms \( \rho \colon P_1 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \to Q \) and \( \sigma \colon Q \to P_1 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \) by \( \rho = \pi_Q\varphi \) and \( \sigma = \varphi^{-1}\iota_Q \).
  Then \( \rho \) is a retraction with a section \( \sigma \).
  Since \( Q \) is irreducible, applying \cref{lem:avoid} recursively yields an appropriate \( B \).
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:other}
  Let \( B \), \( C \), \( Q \), \( R \) be local algebras over a splitting field.
  Assume that there exists an isomorphism
  \[
    \varphi \colon B \otimes C \to Q \otimes R.
  \]
  If \( \pi_Q\varphi\iota_B \colon B \to Q \) is surjective, then so is \( \pi_C\varphi^{-1}\iota_R \colon R \to C \).
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
It suffices to prove that \( T_C = \operatorname{Im} T_{\pi_C\varphi^{-1}\iota_R} \).
  Since \( Q = \operatorname{Im} \pi_Q\varphi\iota_B \) by assumption, \( T_Q = \operatorname{Im} T_{\pi_Q\varphi\iota_B} \).
  Taking preimages of both sides under \( T_{\pi_Q} \colon T_{Q \otimes R} \to T_Q \) yields
  \begin{align*}
    T_{Q \otimes R}
    &= \operatorname{Im} T_{\varphi\iota_B} + \operatorname{Ker} T_{\pi_Q} \\
    &= \operatorname{Im} T_{\varphi\iota_B} + \operatorname{Im} T_{\iota_R}.
  \end{align*}
  Applying \( T_{\pi_C\varphi^{-1}} \colon T_{Q \otimes R} \to T_C \) yields
  \begin{align*}
    & T_{\pi_C\varphi^{-1}}(T_{Q \otimes R}) = \operatorname{Im} T_{\pi_C} = T_C, \\
    & T_{\pi_C\varphi^{-1}}(\operatorname{Im} T_{\varphi\iota_B}) = \operatorname{Im} T_{\pi_C\iota_B} = 0, \\
    & T_{\pi_C\varphi^{-1}}(\operatorname{Im} T_{\iota_R}) = \operatorname{Im} T_{\pi_C\varphi^{-1}\iota_R}.
  \end{align*}
  Hence \( T_C = \operatorname{Im} T_{\pi_C\varphi^{-1}\iota_R} \).
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:ind}
  Let \( P_1, \dotsc, P_n \), \( Q \), \( R \) be local algebras over a splitting field.
  Assume that \( Q \) is irreducible, \( \dim P_i \leq \dim Q \) for every \( i \) and
  \[
    P_1 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \cong Q \otimes R.
  \]
  Then, after reordering indices, we have
  \[
    P_1 \cong Q
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    P_2 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \cong R.
  \]
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let \( \varphi \colon P_1 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \to Q \otimes R \) be an isomorphism.
  Since \( Q \) is irreducible, after reordering indices, \( \pi_Q\varphi\iota_B \colon B \to Q \) is surjective with \( B = P_1 \) by \cref{prop:first}.
  Set \( C = P_2 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \).
  Then \( \pi_C\varphi^{-1}\iota_R \colon R \to C \) is also surjective by \cref{prop:other}.

  Since \( \dim B \leq \dim Q \) and \( \dim C \geq \dim R \) by assumption, the surjective homomorphisms \( B \to Q \) and \( R \to C \) are isomorphisms.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We prove uniqueness by induction on \( \min(n, m) \geq 0 \).
  The base case \( \min(n, m) = 0 \) is clear.

  For the induction step \( \min(n, m) \geq 1 \), we may assume that \( Q_1 \) has the maximum dimension among the tensor factors so that \( \dim P_i \leq \dim Q_1 \) for every \( i \).
  Recall that if an algebra is local and splits, then the same holds for tensor factors.
  Since \( Q_1 \) is irreducible, after reordering indices, we have
  \[
    P_1 \cong Q_1
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    P_2 \otimes \dotsb \otimes P_n \cong Q_2 \otimes \dotsb \otimes Q_m
  \]
  by \cref{prop:ind}.
  Hence uniqueness follows from the induction hypothesis.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- rmk-1: body_md -->
\label{rmk:comm}
  Commutativity is not explicitly stated in Horst's paper~\cite{Ho87}.
  However, the proof of \cite[Lemma~3]{Ho87} appears to rely on Krull's intersection theorem.
  Since Jacobson's conjecture remains open, we regard the algebras studied in~\cite{Ho87} as commutative.
  This interpretation is also compatible with the fact that the paper is assigned classification codes for commutative algebra in MathSciNet and zbMATH Open.
<!-- end rmk-1 -->
<!-- rmk-2: body_md -->
\label{rmk:char}
  N\"usken \cite[p.~527]{Nu02} already noted that some intermediate results of Horst~\cite{Ho87} fail in positive characteristic.
  For completeness, we record counterexamples.
  Let \( F \) be a field of positive characteristic \( p \) and let \( G \) be a cyclic group generated by an element \( g \) of order \( p \).
  \index{\( G \) : Group} 
  \index{\( g \) : Element} 
  \index{\( p \) : Integer} 
  Set \( A = B = FG \) and define the homomorphism \( \varphi \colon A \to A \otimes B \) by \( \varphi(g) = g \otimes g \).
  Then \( \pi_A \varphi \colon A \to A \) is an automorphism and \( \operatorname{Ker} \pi_B\varphi \neq J_A \).
  In particular, \cite[Lemma~4]{Ho87} fails without assuming characteristic zero.
<!-- end rmk-2 -->
<!-- mainthm-2: body_md -->
Let \( F \) be a field of positive characteristic \( p \) and let \( G \) and \( H \) be finite \( p \)-groups.
  Then
  \[
    FG \cong FH \implies F[G/G_\textup{A}] \cong F[H/H_\textup{A}].
  \]
<!-- end mainthm-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
It follows from \cite[Proposition~C]{GL24} that \( FG_\textup{A} \cong FH_\textup{A} \).
  Since
  \[
    F[G/G_\textup{A}] \otimes FG_\textup{A} \cong FG \cong FH \cong F[H/H_\textup{A}] \otimes FH_\textup{A},
  \]
  \cref{main:cor} yields \( F[G/G_\textup{A}] \cong F[H/H_\textup{A}] \).
<!-- end proof-10 -->
